title: Adequacy of the drop-safety predicates
plain_claim: For every toy state `m`: `Inv m` holds iff the container's drop glue run with non-panicking destructors (`containerDrop noPanicDtors m`) does not reach UB. For every frame `es` and state `m`: `DropSafe es m` holds iff unwinding `es` from `m` with non-panicking destructors (`unwindEntries noPanicDtors es m`) ends in `.ok m'` for some `m'` satisfying `Inv`.

hypotheses.name: destructor table fixed to `noPanicDtors` (part of both statements)
hypotheses.purpose: With panicking destructors, drop glue can abort before reaching UB, and unwinding a drop-safe frame can abort.
hypotheses.witness_class: a two-cell state holding one value twice, and a one-local frame, with the destructor table `dtPanicsOn0`

nonvacuity_witness: Both sides true: `containerDrop_pos` (on `ceMem2`, which satisfies `Inv`) and `dropSafe_pos_guardRepairs`; both sides false: `containerDrop_neg_doubleDrop` and `dropSafe_neg_localDuplicates`.
non_claims: Says nothing about panicking destructors; with the table `dtPanicsOn0` both characterizations fail (`dropSafety_adequacy_fails_with_panickingDtors`).
Says nothing about the counters `ctrA` and `ctrB`, which `Inv` ignores.

`DropSafe` treats the frame's guards as pure `(buf, len)` fix-ups; that guard fix-ups and local drops can be applied in either order is a consequence of this restriction of the model. Guard fix-ups (`Guard.fix`) are pure functions of `(buf, len)`: a guard cannot run element destructors, panic, read or change the drop log, or reach UB. Guards that drop elements (for instance a drain's drop guard) are not programs of `Prog`; this result says nothing about them.

Does not say that `Inv` is the right invariant for any real container. Model–system relation: none proved. These are statements about the toy model; they neither establish nor refute the corresponding claims about Rust, its standard library, or any Rust program.
prior_art: The Rustonomicon, rust-lang/nomicon b0bb569883a3e65ab19d4f1adf1b8dbc1629d0a6, src/exception-safety.md L25: 'We need only guarantee that it's a *safe* state.' derived (modeling bridge): `Inv` and `DropSafe` are the toy's 'safe state' predicates.
design_question: What exactly must hold of the state that drop glue will see. Unsafe library code breaks a container's safety invariant temporarily and calls user code in between, and under unwinding drop glue then runs on the broken state. What must hold at each user-code call site, which repair patterns (drop guards, leak amplification, abort-on-panic) are sound in the toy and what each costs, and what a safe API can never rely on once leaking is safe?

title: Unwinding exposes the raw-move intermediate state
plain_claim: Under `unwind`, `rawRetain` run on the container `ceMem2` (values `0`, `1`; it satisfies `Inv`) with callback table `ceCbRemoveThenPanic` (remove element `0`, then panic) and non-panicking destructors unwinds to a state whose `len` still covers the dropped value `0`, which violates `Inv`, and the owner's drop of the container (`harness`) then reaches UB (value `0` dropped twice); under `abort` the same run aborts.
nonvacuity_witness: The instance itself; `rawRetain_unwind_duplicate` is a second instance in which a moved-out slot duplicates value `1`.
non_claims: Does not say every callback panic breaks `rawRetain`: by R3, an unwound state satisfies `Inv` when nothing was removed up to and including the panic (example: `rawRetain_unwind_noRemoval_example`).
Does not claim that any version of the Rust standard library's `retain` or `String::retain` has this behaviour.

The UB in the toy is a double drop of a value. The toy does not model `String`; this result is not a statement about CVE-2020-36317 (https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2020-36317), which is cited for context. Model–system relation: none proved. These are statements about the toy model; they neither establish nor refute the corresponding claims about Rust, its standard library, or any Rust program.

title: Raw moves are exactly correct under `abort`
plain_claim: For every callback table `cb`, every destructor table `dt` and every entry state `m` satisfying `Inv`: `rawRetain` run under `abort` returns a state `m'` with `RetainReturns (specRetain cb dt (toks m.elems)) m m'` (the first `len` cells hold exactly the kept values in order, the removed values are prepended to the drop log, and `Inv m'` holds) if and only if the abstract run `specRetain` finishes; otherwise it aborts; it never reaches UB. Consequently (`rawRetain_panicSafe_abort`) `rawRetain` is panic-safe under `abort`.

hypotheses.purpose: The entry container is well-formed.
hypotheses.witness_class: a two-cell state holding one value twice, with a keep-everything callback

hypotheses.name: panic mode `.abort` (fixed in `rawRetain_abort_exact`; the mode parameter of the corollary `rawRetain_panicSafe_abort`)
hypotheses.purpose: Under `abort` no drop glue runs after a panic, so the broken intermediate state is never observed.
hypotheses.witness_class: the same operation under `unwind` on a two-element container

depth_note: loop invariant over the meta-level recursion of `rawLoop`
nonvacuity_witness: Abort branch: `rawAbortExact_pos` (three elements: remove, keep, panic). Return branch: `rawAbortExact_return_pos` (remove `0`, keep `1` and `2`). Both include `Inv ceMem3`.
non_claims: Buffer cells at index `len` and beyond after return are unspecified.
Says nothing about `unwind` (R1, R3).

The toy's `abort` mode is a property of one run. In Rust the panic strategy is chosen for a whole build: RFC 1513 (text/1513-less-unwinding.md L143-144) requires the `-C panic` mode of the panic runtime to match the final product (outputs that are not rlibs), so library code cannot choose abort-on-panic for itself. derived (modeling bridge); not proved here.

'Panic-safe under abort' holds because an abort is counted as an acceptable outcome (`ResOk .abort`), not because the state at the panic is consistent. Model–system relation: none proved. These are statements about the toy model; they neither establish nor refute the corresponding claims about Rust, its standard library, or any Rust program.

title: Which panics expose the raw-move state
plain_claim: For every callback table, every destructor table and every entry state `m` satisfying `Inv`: if `rawRetain` under `unwind` unwinds to `m'`, then `m'` satisfies `Inv` iff the abstract retain removed no element up to and including the panic, i.e. `(specRetain cb dt (toks m.elems)).rejected = []` (a removed element whose destructor panics counts as removed).

hypotheses.purpose: The entry container is well-formed.
hypotheses.witness_class: a two-cell state holding one value twice, with a panic before any removal

hypotheses.name: h : run .unwind cb dt rawRetain m = .unwound m'
hypotheses.purpose: Binds `m'` to the unwound state of the run.

depth_note: counting argument: after a removal, the `len` cells hold values of the entry container and cannot all be distinct and live
nonvacuity_witness: Right-hand side true and `Inv m'`: `rawRetain_unwind_noRemoval_example`; removal and `¬ Inv m'`: `rawRetain_unwind_doubleDrop`. Both start from states satisfying `Inv`.
non_claims: The informal phrasing 'a callback that panics at step i causes a double drop' is false for panics before any removal (`rawRetain_unwind_noRemoval_example`).

By R3, a destructor panic on the first removed element already yields an unwound state violating `Inv`, because that element counts as removed (`specRetain_example_dtorPanic` shows the abstract result of such a run).

With panicking destructors, the owner's later drop of a state violating `Inv` may abort instead of reaching UB (`dropSafety_adequacy_fails_with_panickingDtors`); R0 covers non-panicking destructors. Model–system relation: none proved. These are statements about the toy model; they neither establish nor refute the corresponding claims about Rust, its standard library, or any Rust program.

title: Call-site characterization
plain_claim: For every toy program `p`: `p` is panic-safe under `unwind` (for every callback table, destructor table and entry state satisfying `Inv`, the run `run .unwind cb dt p m` reaches no UB and a return or an unwind leaves `Inv`) iff (a) `p` is panic-safe under `abort`, and (b) for every callback table, destructor table and entry state satisfying `Inv`, every user-code site reached by `p` (callback invocations and element-destructor invocations, as produced by the interpreter `exec` through `sites`) satisfies `DropSafe`: after the frame's guard fix-ups are applied to `(buf, len)`, the fixed-up `len` is at most the buffer length, and the values of the live locals together with the first `len` cells of the fixed-up buffer are initialized, pairwise distinct and not in the drop log. `run` and `sites` start the interpreter with an empty frame, and guard fix-ups are pure functions of `(buf, len)`.

hypotheses.name: PanicSafe .abort p (right-hand-side conjunct)
hypotheses.purpose: The normal-execution path must itself be correct; call sites do not see it.
hypotheses.witness_class: a program with no user-code site (`badSetLen`)

hypotheses.name: CallSitesDropSafe p, including destructor sites (right-hand-side conjunct)
hypotheses.purpose: Unwinding may start at any user-code call, including element destructors.
hypotheses.witness_class: a two-instruction program with one destructor site (`truncateLate`) and a one-element container

hypotheses.name: entry precondition Inv m inside CallSitesDropSafe
hypotheses.purpose: Sites reached from states violating `Inv` are irrelevant to panic safety, which also assumes `Inv` on entry.
hypotheses.witness_class: a two-cell entry state holding one value twice

hypotheses.name: quantifier over all destructor tables inside CallSitesDropSafe
hypotheses.purpose: Readability; equivalent to fixing `noPanicDtors` (`callSitesDropSafe_iff_noPanicDtors`).

depth_note: right to left by induction on `Prog`; left to right by table surgery at the site (a panicking callback invocation, or a destructor that panics on exactly one value)
nonvacuity_witness: Both sides hold: `truncateThenCall_satisfies_both_sides` (with one destructor site and one callback site, `truncateThenCall_sites_example`). Both sides fail: `rawRetain_not_callSitesDropSafe` and `panicSafe_neg_rawRetain`.
non_claims: Guard fix-ups (`Guard.fix`) are pure functions of `(buf, len)`: a guard cannot run element destructors, panic, read or change the drop log, or reach UB. Guards that drop elements (for instance a drain's drop guard) are not programs of `Prog`; this result says nothing about them.
Says nothing about callers that hold guards or locals with drop glue over the same container; whether the characterization would then need the caller's frame as well is not proved here.
The model has no catch boundary: after an unwind the state is handed to the owner, whose drop glue runs (`harness`); reuse of the container after a caught panic is not modelled.

Says nothing about concurrency, re-entrant callbacks, user code with effects other than return or panic, non-terminating operations (every `Prog` run terminates), or unwinding across a foreign-function boundary (which the Rust Reference lists as undefined behaviour; not modelled).
`DropSafe` is a memory-safety condition in the toy; it says nothing about logical invariants (R15).

The bounded check covers nine sample programs on a finite family of tables and states; the unbounded statement is the theorem. Model–system relation: none proved. These are statements about the toy model; they neither establish nor refute the corresponding claims about Rust, its standard library, or any Rust program.

title: Destructor sites count as call sites
plain_claim: The program `truncateLate` (drop the last element, then decrement `len`) is panic-safe under `abort` and satisfies `CallbackSitesDropSafe`, yet it fails `CallSitesDropSafe` and is not panic-safe under `unwind` (`truncateLate_counterexample`). From every state (not only states satisfying `Inv`), under every callback table and every destructor table, every user-code site that `truncateLate` reaches (as produced by `exec` through `sites`) is an element-destructor site, so it reaches no callback site (`truncateLate_sites_destructor`). On the one-element container `ceMem1`, which satisfies `Inv`, with the destructor table `dtPanicsOn0`, under `unwind` and every callback table, `truncateLate` unwinds to the state `⟨[some 0], 1, [0], 0, 0⟩` (buffer `[some 0]`, `len = 1`, drop log `[0]`): the panicking destructor leaves `len` covering the cell of the dropped value `0`, and that state violates `Inv` (`truncateLate_dtorPanic_unwound`).
nonvacuity_witness: The statement has no hypotheses. The destructor-panic run behind its `¬ PanicSafe .unwind truncateLate` conjunct, on `ceMem1` (which satisfies `Inv`) with `dtPanicsOn0`, is stated by `truncateLate_dtorPanic_unwound`.
non_claims: `truncateLate_dtorPanic_unwound` describes one entry state (`ceMem1`) and one destructor table (`dtPanicsOn0`); it states nothing about other entry states or destructor tables.

Does not say that dropping before updating `len` is unsafe when destructors cannot panic (`truncateLate_panicSafeAssumingNoDtorPanic`). Model–system relation: none proved. These are statements about the toy model; they neither establish nor refute the corresponding claims about Rust, its standard library, or any Rust program.

title: Leak amplification is sound but leaks
plain_claim: For every callback table, every destructor table (panicking destructors included) and every entry state `m` satisfying `Inv`: `leakRetain` (set `len := 0`, run the raw loop, restore `len`) under `unwind` returns a state satisfying `RetainReturns (specRetain cb dt (toks m.elems)) m` if and only if `specRetain` finishes; otherwise it unwinds to a state with `len = 0`, drop log equal to the abstract `rejected` list prepended to the entry drop log, and unchanged buffer length and counters; it never aborts or reaches UB. Consequently it is panic-safe under `unwind` (`leakRetain_panicSafe_unwind`), and (`leakRetain_unwound_leaks`, same hypotheses, for an unwound state `m'`) the first `len` cells of `m'` hold no value and an entry value is in the drop log of `m'` iff the abstract retain removed it; so every entry value that was not removed is leaked (neither in the drop log nor held by the container).

title: A drop guard updated before each destructor is exact on unwind
plain_claim: For every callback table, every destructor table (panicking destructors included) and every entry state `m` satisfying `Inv`: `guardRetain` (a back-shift guard whose fields are updated before each removed element's destructor runs) under `unwind` returns a state satisfying `RetainReturns (specRetain cb dt (toks m.elems)) m` if and only if `specRetain` finishes; otherwise it unwinds to a state `m'` whose first `len` cells hold exactly the kept values followed by the unprocessed values (`toks m'.elems = kept ++ rest`), with drop log `rejected ++ m.dropped` and `Inv m'`; it never aborts or reaches UB.

hypotheses.purpose: The entry container is well-formed.
hypotheses.witness_class: a two-cell state holding one value twice, with a keep-everything callback

non_claims: No hypothesis on element destructors is needed for this guard ordering; this does not extend to guards updated after the destructor (R9).

Does not cover the owner's later drop of the container while the panic propagates. In the toy, a destructor that panics there makes `containerDrop` return `.abort` by definition (`guardRetain_ownerDrop_doublePanic_aborts_example`: the guard has repaired the container, then the owner's drop aborts); that is a modelling choice, not a theorem about Rust.
`GuardUnwindExact` does not state that the buffer length and the counters are unchanged (unlike `LeakUnwindExact`); buffer cells at index `len` and beyond are unspecified.

The back-shift guard runs no destructor (its fix-up is a memory move and a `len` update); the toy guard omits the `set_len(0)` that std's `retain_mut` also performs. Omitting it relies on the guard staying in the library frame, where no instruction of user code can forget it (in `Prog`, user code is a callback table); a guard that safe code could forget is the situation of R11, and what `guardRetain` would then need is not proved here. Model–system relation: none proved. These are statements about the toy model; they neither establish nor refute the corresponding claims about Rust, its standard library, or any Rust program.

title: The guard is leak-free on unwind
plain_claim: For every callback table, every destructor table and every entry state `m` satisfying `Inv`: if `guardRetain` under `unwind` unwinds to `m'`, then every value held by the first `len` cells of `m` is in the drop log of `m'` or held by the first `len` cells of `m'` (`LeakFree m m'`).

title: The toy destructor-reliant drain reaches UB once `forgetGuard` is available
plain_claim: In the toy client language, all of whose instructions are safe operations, the client `forgetClient` = `[.drain, .next, .dropVal, .forgetGuard]` (drain, take one value, drop it, forget the guard) run against the destructor-reliant drain on the one-element container `ceMem1` (which satisfies `Inv`) reaches UB (the owner's drop drops value `0` a second time).
nonvacuity_witness: The instance itself; `leakAmplifiedDrain_forgetClient_ok` runs the same client against the leak-amplified drain without UB.
non_claims: A statement about one API and one client in one toy client language; it does not prove that every destructor-reliant API is unsound.

Of the positive controls, R12 and R13 are about the client language; R14 (`closureScopedDrain_panicSafe_unwind`) is about `drainWith`, a program of `Prog`, in which user code is a callback table and has no instruction that reaches the library's guard. R14 therefore does not run the client `forgetClient` or any other client program.
The toy shows a sequential double drop and has no threads; it is not a statement about rust-lang/rust issue 24292 (https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/24292), which is cited for context.
`Rc` cycles are not modelled; safe `forget` stands in for every safe way to leak.
The client language has no panics and non-panicking destructors.

Escape hatches not modelled: types that cannot be leaked (linear rather than affine types), and the `Pin` drop guarantee, which requires `drop` to run before the memory of a pinned value is invalidated or reused (std 1.85.0 `std::pin` documentation) while still allowing pinned values to be leaked. Model–system relation: none proved. These are statements about the toy model; they neither establish nor refute the corresponding claims about Rust, its standard library, or any Rust program.

rust-lang/rust issue 24292, https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/24292 (2015), cited by URL for context.
The Rustonomicon, rust-lang/nomicon b0bb569883a3e65ab19d4f1adf1b8dbc1629d0a6, src/leaking.md L36-37: 'However *unsafe* code cannot rely on destructors to be run in order to be safe.'

The Rust Reference, rust-lang/reference c9cc32825b03fc206d9c6fe73e9ca6a2f3576d6c, src/behavior-not-considered-unsafe.md L6: 'Leaks of memory and other resources' and L7: 'Exiting without calling destructors'.

Rust std 1.85.0, `std::mem::forget` documentation (source rust-lang/rust 4d91de4e48198da2e33413efdcd9cd2cc0c46688, library/core/src/mem/mod.rs L52-53): 'Because forgetting a value is allowed, any `unsafe` code you write must allow for this possibility.' derived (modeling bridge).

title: A closure-scoped drain is panic-safe under unwinding
plain_claim: For every callback table (callbacks may drop or forget each element they receive, or panic while owning it), every destructor table, and every entry state satisfying `Inv`: the closure-scoped drain `drainWith`, which keeps its guard in the library frame, run under `unwind`, reaches no UB, and a return or an unwind leaves `Inv` (`PanicSafe .unwind drainWith`).

hypotheses.name: Inv m (inside PanicSafe)
hypotheses.purpose: The entry container is well-formed.
hypotheses.witness_class: a two-cell state holding one value twice (unwinds to a non-`Inv` state), and a one-cell container with an uninitialized cell (UB)

depth_note: loop invariant: the buffer is never modified, and every value added to the drop log comes from an index below the cursor
nonvacuity_witness: `closureScopedDrain_example` (entry `ceMem3` satisfies `Inv`; forget one element, panic while holding the next; the unprocessed element stays in the container).
non_claims: `drainWith` is a program of `Prog`, not of the client language of R11-R13; user code in `Prog` has no instruction that reaches the library's guard, so 'the guard cannot be forgotten' holds by construction. The callbacks can forget elements (`forgetVal`).
The theorem is panic safety (`ResOk`); it gives no functional specification of `drainWith`.

On unwind the toy guard moves the unprocessed elements back to the front of the container; it does not model guards that drop them. Guard fix-ups (`Guard.fix`) are pure functions of `(buf, len)`: a guard cannot run element destructors, panic, read or change the drop log, or reach UB. Guards that drop elements (for instance a drain's drop guard) are not programs of `Prog`; this result says nothing about them.

Not modelled: asynchronous closure-scoped APIs, where a suspended future can be leaked; and deallocating a stack frame without running its destructors (for instance with C `longjmp`), which the Rust Reference says the runtime assumes does not happen.

Not a proof about `std::thread::scope`. Model–system relation: none proved. These are statements about the toy model; they neither establish nor refute the corresponding claims about Rust, its standard library, or any Rust program.
